A.explanation: Dividing by 4 has no physical basis because frequency is proportional to $1/\lambda$ for fixed wave speed, and $\lambda$ gets smaller for higher maxima.

B.explanation: This would be the second harmonic of an open-open tube, but a closed-open tube cannot have even multiples of $f_1$ because the node-antinode condition is lost.

C.explanation: This assumes every integer multiple $f_1, 2f_1, 3f_1, 4f_1$ resonates, which applies to a tube open at both ends, not to a tube closed at one end.

D.explanation: The fourth closed-pipe resonance fits $7$ quarter-wavelengths in the tube, so $f_4 = 7f_1$ with the same wave speed.

hints: Notice the stated end conditions: displacement node at the closed end and antinode at the open end for the first loud maximum at $f_1$.
Recall that tube length $L$ is fixed, so each resonance must fit an odd number of quarter-wavelengths: $L = \lambda/4, 3\lambda/4, 5\lambda/4...$.
Use $v = f\lambda$ with constant $v$ to connect the fourth allowed wavelength to $f_1$ by counting how $\lambda$ changes from the first to the fourth fit.
walkthrough: Identify the first resonance: node at closed end and antinode at open end means the tube length holds one quarter-wave, so $L = \lambda_1/4$.
Next resonances must keep the same node-antinode ends, so add half-wavelengths: $L = 3\lambda_2/4$ for the second maximum, $L = 5\lambda_3/4$ for the third, $L = 7\lambda_4/4$ for the fourth.
Hence only odd harmonics exist: frequencies are $f = v/\lambda = (2n-1)v/(4L)$ for $n = 1,2,3,4$.
